subject: sociology
chapter_title: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society

concepts.title: Demography and Social Demography
concepts.section: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society
concepts.definition: Demography is the systematic study of population -- the word joins the Greek demos and graphein, describing people -- covering changes in population size, patterns of births, deaths and migration, and the structure and composition of the population; social demography goes further, asking how social processes and structures regulate these demographic processes and tracing the social reasons behind population trends.
concepts.key_idea: Numbers about people are never just natural facts -- society shapes how they are born, die and move.
question_patterns: define demography and state its main concerns
how does social demography differ from formal demography
why do social demographers study population trends through social reasons
name the components of population structure that demographers examine
is population merely an obstacle to development, discuss
what is meant by describing demography as a systematic study of population

solution_steps.explain: demos plus graphein means describing people; the discipline tracks size, vital events and composition over time
formal demography measures rates and structures, while social demography enquires into the wider causes and consequences of these patterns
social processes and structures regulate demographic processes, so trends in births, deaths and migration carry social explanations

worked_examples.q: What is the systematic study of population called?

concepts.title: Malthusian Theory of Population Growth
concepts.section: 2.1 The Malthusian Theory of Population Growth
concepts.definition: In his 1798 Essay, Malthus argued that populations grow in geometric progression like 2, 4, 8, 16 while subsistence grows only in arithmetic progression like 2, 4, 6, 8, so humanity is condemned to poverty unless population growth is checked -- by preventive checks such as postponed marriage or abstinence, or by positive checks like famine and disease that he saw as nature's correction; history refuted him as food production and living standards rose alongside population, and critics blamed unequal distribution rather than births for poverty.
concepts.key_idea: The race between a multiplying population and a linearly growing food supply defined the pessimism -- and the European record disproved it.
question_patterns: state the main argument of the malthusian theory of population growth
distinguish geometric and arithmetic progression as malthus used them
differentiate preventive checks from positive checks with examples
why were malthus's predictions proved false by european experience
how did liberal and marxist scholars criticise malthus on poverty
why did malthus consider famines and diseases inevitable

solution_steps.explain: population was said to double geometrically while agriculture could only add arithmetically, so subsistence would always be overtaken
preventive checks like late marriage and celibacy operate through human will, while positive checks -- famine and disease -- were nature's answer to the food-population imbalance

late nineteenth century Europe saw birth rates fall and epidemics controlled, agricultural productivity rose, and scholars such as liberal and Marxist critics argued that unequal distribution of resources, not population growth, causes poverty

worked_examples.q: Malthus said population grows in which progression: geometric or arithmetic?

concepts.title: Theory of Demographic Transition and India's Incomplete Transition
concepts.definition: Demographic transition links population growth to economic development through three stages: a backward stage of low growth where both birth and death rates are high, a transitional stage of explosive growth when death rates fall fast while reproductive behaviour adjusts slowly, and a developed stage of low growth where both rates are low; India sits in the middle -- mortality has been cut by disease control and public health, but the socioculturally sticky birth rate lags behind, so the transition is not yet complete.
concepts.key_idea: Deaths respond quickly to medicine and sanitation; births respond slowly to prosperity and education -- the gap between them is the population explosion.
question_patterns: describe the three stages of demographic transition
why does a population explosion occur in the transitional stage
why is india's demographic transition called incomplete
why does the death rate fall faster than the birth rate
how is population growth linked to economic development in transition theory
compare the first and third stages of demographic transition

solution_steps.explain: in the underdeveloped, technologically backward society growth is low because death and birth rates are both very high, leaving a small net difference
disease control, public health and nutrition bring deaths down quickly, but reproductive behaviour evolved under high-mortality poverty changes slowly, so growth spikes
developed societies reach low-low equilibrium; in India mortality fell after 1921 while the birth rate only declined slightly, keeping the transition unfinished

worked_examples.q: In which stage of demographic transition do death rates fall while birth rates stay high?

concepts.title: Demographic Concepts and Indicators as Rates
concepts.definition: Demographic concepts are expressed as rates or ratios -- two numbers, one a statistic for an area and period, the other a standard of comparison: birth rate counts live births per 1000 population, death rate counts deaths per 1000, growth rate is their difference, fertility rate counts births per 1000 women aged 15-49, infant mortality per 1000 live births, maternal mortality per 100,000 live births, life expectancy estimates average years of survival, and sex ratio gives females per 1000 males.
concepts.key_idea: Every headline number about population is a ratio against a standard -- read the denominator before believing the story.
question_patterns: define birth rate and death rate as demographic indicators
how is the rate of natural increase of population computed
when is a population said to have reached replacement level
distinguish fertility rate from birth rate
why are infant and maternal mortality called indicators of backwardness
how is life expectancy calculated and what does it mean

solution_steps.explain: divide the event count for an area and year by the population measured in thousands to get events per 1000 population
subtract the death rate from the birth rate; a zero or near-zero difference signals a stabilised population at replacement level
females per 1000 males is the standard gender-balance indicator for an area and time

worked_examples.q: Birth rate counts live births per how many of the population?

concepts.title: Size and Growth of India's Population
concepts.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population
concepts.definition: Census 2011 counted 121 crores of Indians, second only to China; growth was modest before 1951 -- never above 1.33 per cent a year and actually negative at -0.03 per cent in 1911-21 when the influenza pandemic killed about 5 per cent of the population -- then jumped to 2.2 per cent during 1961-81 before easing; deaths fell as epidemics and famines were controlled, with Amartya Sen's failure-of-entitlements insight showing famine is about inability to obtain food, while the birth rate declines slowly and unevenly, from below-replacement TFRs in Kerala or Tamil Nadu to 3.3 in Bihar.
concepts.key_idea: India's growth curve bends around disasters and medicine: epidemics and famine once cut numbers, disease control then exploded them, and fertility now declines state by state.
question_patterns: what was india's population according to census 2011
why did india record a negative growth rate during 1911-1921
trace the trend of india's population growth rate after independence
what caused the decline in the death rate after 1921
explain amartya sen's idea of failure of entitlements regarding famines
compare total fertility rates of kerala and bihar and their significance

solution_steps.explain: annual growth stayed below 1.33 per cent up to 1951 and turned negative in 1911-21 as the Spanish flu killed some 12.5 million people, about 5 per cent of the population

control of epidemics like plague, smallpox and cholera, mass vaccination, sanitation and better famine relief -- reinforced by irrigation and communication -- cut the death rate sharply while birth rates only edged down

prosperity, falling infant mortality and education pull fertility down, so Andhra Pradesh, Himachal, Punjab, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal reached TFRs of 1.7 and Kerala sits below replacement, while Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh remain high, set to supply half of India's population additions to 2041

worked_examples.q: Census 2011 counted how many crores of Indians?

concepts.title: Age Structure, Dependency Ratio and the Demographic Dividend
concepts.section: 2.3 Age Structure of the Indian Population
concepts.definition: India's population is young: the under-15 share fell from 42 per cent in 1971 to 29 per cent in 2011 while the 60-plus share rose from 5 to 7 per cent, and projections to 2026 give 23, 64 and 12 per cent for the young, working and old groups; the dependency ratio compares dependents -- those below 15 and above 64 -- with the 15-64 working-age group, and its fall from 79 in 1970 toward a projected 48 in 2025 opens a demographic dividend that turns into growth only if education and employment employ the new workers.
concepts.key_idea: A bulge of workers supports growth only while jobs and schools absorb them; otherwise the dividend matures into a burden of ageing.
question_patterns: how has the age composition of india changed since 1971
define dependency ratio and explain its computation
what is the demographic dividend and why is it temporary
why does the age pyramid of india show a middle bulge for 2026
why is nothing automatic about india's demographic advantage
compare the projected age pyramids of kerala and uttar pradesh

solution_steps.explain: the 0-14 group slid from 42 to 29 per cent between 1971 and 2011 and is projected at 23 per cent by 2026, while the 60-plus group climbs from 5 toward 12 per cent, and employment growth for 15-30 year olds collapsed from about 2.4 per cent a year to under 1 per cent
dependents are those below 15 or above 64; the ratio to the working-age population fell from 79 in 1970 to 64 in 2005 and is projected at 48 in 2025 before ageing pushes it back to 50 by 2050
the dividend is a potential, realised only when rising education and employment convert workers into earners -- unemployment turns entrants back into dependents

worked_examples.q: The dependency ratio compares dependents with which age group: 15-64 or 0-6?

concepts.title: The Declining Sex Ratio and the Child Sex Ratio Crisis
concepts.definition: Nature produces about 943-952 girls per 1000 boys and girls' disease resistance and women's longer lives give most societies a sex ratio near 1050 females per 1000 males, but India's ratio slid for a century from 972 in 1901 to 927 in 1991, recovering only to 933 in 2001 and 943 in 2011; more alarming is the child sex ratio for 0-6 years, which plunged 18 points from 945 to 927 during 1991-2001 and fell again to 919 in 2011, a collapse tied to son preference and the neglect of girl babies under norms that value males more.
concepts.key_idea: A country where females should outnumber males shows the opposite -- and the youngest cohort is worst, signalling discrimination before birth and after.
question_patterns: define sex ratio and give its trend in india since 1901
why do most societies show a sex ratio favourable to females
what is the child sex ratio and why is its fall alarming
link son preference to the declining sex ratio in india
compare the overall and child sex ratios of census 2011
which social norms are blamed for the neglect of girl babies

solution_steps.explain: about 943-952 girls are born per 1000 boys, and girls' infancy advantage plus women's longevity usually lift the ratio to roughly 1050
the overall ratio fell from 972 in 1901 to an all-time low of 927 in 1991, then rose modestly to 933 in 2001 and 943 in 2011

the 0-6 sex ratio dropped 18 points from 945 to 927 in 1991-2001, slipping below the overall ratio for the first time, and sank further to 919 in 2011, reflecting son preference and relative neglect of girls

worked_examples.q: India's sex ratio in 2011 stood at how many females per 1000 males?

concepts.title: Literacy: Levels, Gaps and the Reproduction of Inequality
concepts.definition: Literacy empowers -- it widens career consciousness, health awareness and participation in the knowledge economy -- and about two-thirds of Indians are now literate, but the gains lag population growth and are uneven: women trail men by 16.3 percentage points in 2011 even though female literacy rose faster, at 10.4 against 7.6 points over 2001-11, Scheduled Castes and Tribes remain behind with their women lowest, and because illiterate parents struggle to educate children, literacy gaps reproduce inequality across generations.
concepts.key_idea: Literacy advances fastest where it started lowest, yet the gaps it must close -- gender, caste, region -- pass themselves on to the next generation.
question_patterns: why is literacy called an instrument of empowerment
compare male and female literacy trends between 2001 and 2011
what is the gender gap in literacy according to census 2011
how do literacy rates vary across social groups in india
why do literacy inequalities reproduce inequality across generations
contrast the literacy positions of kerala and bihar

solution_steps.explain: roughly two-thirds of the population is literate now, though gains must outrun continued population growth

the 2011 female-male gap stood at 16.3 points, female literacy rose 10.4 points against 7.6 for males over 2001-11, and historically disadvantaged communities, especially their women, remain behind with Bihar far from Kerala's near-universal literacy
illiterate parents are severely disadvantaged in securing their children's education, so today's literacy inequality becomes tomorrow's

worked_examples.q: About what share of Indians are literate now: two-thirds or one-tenth?

concepts.title: Rural-Urban Differences and Population Policy in India
concepts.definition: Most Indians -- 68.8 per cent in 2011 -- still live in villages, but the urban share has climbed from about 11 per cent a century ago to 31.2 per cent while agriculture's GDP share fell to about one-sixth; migration to cities follows work, the decay of common property resources and even the anonymity that shelters Scheduled Castes and Tribes from village humiliation, and India, the first country to announce an official population policy in 1952, channels these pressures through the National Family Planning Programme and later goals such as the National Health Policy 2017 target of bringing total fertility to 2.1 by 2025.
concepts.key_idea: Villages empty into metropolises not only for jobs but for dignity, and state policy tries to steer both the movement and the birth rate.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy102.txt 2.6 Rural-Urban Differences, 2.7 Population Policy, Box 2.4 (lines 1041-1265)
question_patterns: compare the rural and urban shares of india's population in 2011
why do rural people migrate to cities besides the search for work
how does the anonymity of the city help oppressed groups
what happened to common property resources and with what effect on villagers
why is india described as a pioneer of population policy
state the key goals of the national health policy 2017

solution_steps.explain: 68.8 per cent rural and 31.2 per cent urban in 2011, with more than two-thirds of urban Indians packed into 27 million-plus cities whose infrastructure strains to keep up

shrinking ponds, forests and grazing lands convert free goods into purchases while village cash income stays scarce, and the city offers work, markets of aspiration via mass media, and anonymity that protects the low-caste and lets dominant-caste poor do low-status work

from the 1952 announcement and National Family Planning Programme to NHP 2017's targets -- TFR 2.1, life expectancy 70, reduced infant and maternal mortality -- policy tries to steer growth in socially desirable directions amid population momentum toward 1.6 billion by 2050

worked_examples.q: What share of Indians lived in villages in 2011: 68.8 percent or 12 percent?

worked_examples.question_pattern: A district records {live_births} live births and {deaths} deaths in a year with a population of {population_thousands} thousand. Find its birth rate, death rate and rate of natural increase.

solution_template.explain: live births divided by population in thousands gives births per 1000 population
the same arithmetic on deaths gives deaths per 1000 population
birth rate minus death rate is the growth rate, and a value near zero would mean replacement level

worked_examples.question_pattern: A population of {working_age_population} thousand people in the 15-64 group must support {dependents} thousand children and elderly. Compute the dependency ratio.

solution_template.explain: dependents divided by the working-age population, expressed as a percentage
a falling ratio, as from 79 in 1970 toward 48 projected for 2025, means fewer mouths per worker -- the demographic dividend window
the benefit materialises only if the working-age majority is educated and employed; joblessness re-creates dependency

worked_examples.question_pattern: Starting from a base of {base}, compare Malthus's geometric population series against an arithmetic food series adding {increment} per period after {periods} rounds.

solution_template.explain: each period doubles the previous total, as in Malthus's 2, 4, 8, 16 series
each period adds a fixed increment, as in Malthus's 2, 4, 6, 8 series
the widening difference between the two series is the trap Malthus predicted, which rising agricultural productivity in fact closed
